Falam Orthography'; = round 1's unopened 'Bibles International 2011 Chin Writers' Handbook']
sources.note: Explicit practical-orthography account of Falam tone (high vs other, marked by diacritics together with vowel length; 'three tones' remark) and an informal claim that each word has one stressed syllable (no position given). The handbook is written for Falam-township writers generally and lists 'Races or Clans in Falam Township' (Hlawnceu, Hualngo, Laizo, Ngawn, Tapawng, Zahau, Khualsim, Lente, Sim, Taisun, Zanniat; p.144) but never names Bualkhaw/Bualkhua/Phadei and describes standard (Laizo/Zahau-based) written Falam only.

sources.citation: Khar Thuan. 2008. A phonological description of Falam Chin. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. 138 pp.
sources.note: For FALAM (Laizo-based Falam-town speech, fala1243), not Bualkhaw: sec.4.2 pp.59-60 'Both stress and intonation are meaningful in their context but they are not contrastive.. It is proposed that Falam stress pattern always occurs in the last syllable of disyllabic word or trisyllabic word'; ch.6 p.94 'Stress patterns fall generally upon the second syllable of a compound word consisting of two syllables, and if the word contains more than two syllables, the stress will fall on the last syllable of the word.' Sec.1.2 p.12 explicitly places Bualkhua OUTSIDE the described group: 'Tapong, Bualkhua…
